Abstract
Background/Aim: Acute cardiovascular changes following cerebral ischemia are significant contributors to stroke‑
related mortality, yet their mechanisms remain poorly understood. Τhis study investigated cardiovascular responses
in a cynomolgus monkey thromboembolic stroke model. 
Materials and Methods: A thromboembolic stroke model was induced in eight male animals (aged 4 to 6 years) by
occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery with an autologous blood clod. Arterial blood pressure, heart rate,
respiratory rate, and body temperature were continuously monitored in conscious, free‑moving animals for 24 h
post‑embolization using a telemetry system. 
Results: Blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate significantly increased following embolization and these
increases persisted for 24 h. Circadian rhythm disruption was suggested by elevated nighttime respiratory rate and
body temperature. Three moribund animals exhibited higher blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate
compared to five non‑moribund animals, along with a drop in body temperature in the hours before death.
Electrocardiographic analysis revealed no major abnormalities in non‑moribund animals, but the moribund animals
showed arrhythmias and ST‑segment elevation before death. 
Conclusion: These cardiovascular changes closely resemble those observed in stroke‑heart syndrome in humans,
highlighting the relevance of this non‑human primate model in studying acute cardiovascular complications following
cerebral ischemia. This model could be applied in the development of therapies for managing post‑stroke
cardiovascular events.
Keywords: Experimental thromboembolic stroke model, cynomolgus monkey, cardiovascular, telemetry.

Introduction
Stroke is the second‑leading cause of death worldwide, with
ischemic stroke accounting for approximately 88% of all
stroke cases (1). The sequelae of ischemic stroke extend
beyond the brain, impacting various organs, including the
cardiovascular system. Acute cardiovascular changes, such
as arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and sudden cardiac
death, are frequent complications in stroke patients (2).
These secondary cardiovascular events significantly
contribute to stroke‑related mortality and long‑term
disability (3) and are collectively termed stroke‑heart
syndrome (SHS) (4). Post‑stroke cardiac complications
seriously affect prognosis and are the second most frequent
cause of death in patients with stroke (4). Therefore,
understanding the interplay between cerebral ischemia and
the cardiovascular system is vital for improving stroke
outcomes and guiding therapeutic interventions.
Approximately 20% of ischemic stroke patients
experience cardiac arrhythmias, and up to 30% exhibit
myocardial injury, often characterized by elevated troponin
levels (5, 6). While these relationships are well‑documented
in clinical settings, research in animal models has typically
focused on the neurological consequences of ischemia, with

limited emphasis on the associated cardiovascular
responses. Rodent models have been the mainstay for
stroke research, providing valuable insights into the
pathophysiology of cerebral ischemia (7) and have also
been used to investigate neurocardiogenic mechanisms in
SHS (8); however, there are anatomical and physiological
differences that limit the translational applicability of
findings from rodent models to clinical practice (9).
Therefore, we developed a non‑human primate (NHP)
thromboembolic stroke model that closely parallels clinical
thromboembolic stroke (10‑14). Despite NHPs having been
used extensively to study neuroprotective strategies and
neurological outcomes following cerebral ischemia, the
acute cardiovascular alterations that accompany cerebral
ischemia in these models remain largely unexplored.
In the present study, we describe the acute cardiovascular
changes that occur following cerebral ischemia in an NHP
thromboembolic stroke model using a telemetry system that
enables simultaneous assessment of cardiovascular
parameters [arterial blood pressure, heart rate, and
electrocardiogram (ECG)] as well as indices of central
nervous system function (body temperature and locomotor
activity) and respiratory system (respiratory rate) in
conscious, free‑moving animals. Furthermore, we evaluated
the relationship between the changes in cardiovascular
parameters after brain ischemia and stroke outcomes.
Materials and Methods
Animal preparation. All procedures in animals were
approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Shin
Nippon Biomedical Laboratories, Ltd., a facility fully
certified by AAALAC International, and the research was
performed in accordance with the Institutional Guidelines
for Animal Experiments and in compliance with the
Japanese Law Concerning the Protection and Control of
Animals (Law No. 105 and Notification No. 6). Procedures
were conducted under veterinary supervision. The
principal investigator and the primate handling staff were
present at all procedures. Thirteen male cynomolgus
monkeys weighing 3 to 6 kg and aged 4 to 6 years old
(Source: Breeding: Guangxi Primate Center of China) were
used. The NHPs were housed in cages 68 cm wide, 62 cm
high, and 77 cm deep (conforming to NIH requirements)
in a room maintained under the following conditions:

temperature: 26±3˚C, humidity: 50%±20%, ventilation:
15 times/h, and a 12‑h light/dark cycle (lighting from
07:00 a.m.).
Telemetry transmitter implantation surgery. To monitor the
physiological parameters, a telemetric transmitter (TL11
M2‑D70‑PCT, Data Sciences International Inc., New
Brighton, MN, USA) was implanted intraperitoneally under
isoflurane inhalation anesthesia (0.5% to 2.0%, Isoflu,
Zoetis Japan Inc., Tokyo, Japan) after animal sedation by an
intramuscular injection of ketamine hydrochloride (Ketalar
for Intramuscular Injection 500 mg, Daiichi Sankyo
Propharma Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan, 50 mg/ml). A telemetric
1994
Yoshikawa et al: Cardiovascular Changes After Brain Ischemia in Non‑human Primate Thromboembolic Stroke Model
catheter for blood pressure measurement was inserted via
the femoral artery and positioned in the abdominal aorta.
The 2 lead wires for ECG (lead II) were implanted
subcutaneously in the right upper and left lateral thorax.
The animals were allowed 2 weeks to recover from surgery.
Physiological parameters, such as blood pressure, heart
rate, ECG, and body temperature, were continually recorded
on a data recorder (RX‑8016, TEAC Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan)
via the telemetry system (Dataquest A.R.T. Data Sciences
International Inc.). All animals received antibiotics [aqueous
suspended injection of dihydrostreptomycin sulfate 
(250 mg potency/ml) and benzylpenicillin procaine
(200,000 units/ml), Meiji Seika Kaisha, Ltd., Tokyo, Japan,
0.05 ml/lg, intramuscular] and were allowed to recover
from the anesthesia.
Monkey thromboembolic stroke model. Eight telemetry
transmitter‑implanted animals were used for the monkey
thromboembolic stroke model. The procedure for
development of the thromboembolic stroke model has been
described previously (10‑14). Briefly, a chronic catheter for
the injection of a blood clot was implanted in the left

internal carotid artery in each animal under isoflurane
inhalation anesthesia, and a single autologous blood clot
(approximately 10 cm in length and 1.0 mm in diameter)
was injected into the left internal carotid artery through the
carotid catheter under light sevoflurane anesthesia. 
In the control group, five telemetry transmitter‑
implanted animals were used as normal controls, and only
inhalation anesthesia, similar to that used for clot
injection, was administered.
Neurologic evaluation. Neurologic deficits according to a
standardized score (10) were assigned at 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 h
after embolization. Of the 100 points possible, 28 were
assigned for consciousness, 22 for the sensory system, 32
for the motor system, and 18 for skeletal muscle
coordination. The total neurologic deficit score was the
sum of the 4 category scores. In normal animals, the score
for each category was 0 points. Neurologic deficit was
assessed blind by an experienced observer. 
Cardiovascular data measurement and analysis. Waveforms
of blood pressure and ECG were continuously recorded
using the telemetry system from approximately 5 h before
to 24 h after embolization, and heart rate and respiratory
rate data were extracted from the blood pressure
waveforms. Blood pressure (systolic and diastolic), heart
rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature were analyzed
for 30 s from the analysis time point [4 h before
embolization (pre), and every hour from immediately (0 h)
to 24 h after embolization]. ECG was analyzed using an ECG
system (SBP‑2000, Softron Co., Ltd., Kanagawa, Japan). The
PR, RR, and QT intervals and QRS duration were measured;
each interval and duration were calculated at each analysis
point (same time point as that for blood pressure, but not
including 0 h) from the averaged continuous ECG
waveforms over an 8‑s period. Corrected QT interval (QTc)
was calculated with the following formula using the ECG
system: (Bazett’s formula) QTc=QT/(RR)1/2.

Statistical analysis. Data on blood pressure, heart rate, ECG
parameters (except RR interval and percentage changes in
QTc interval), respiratory rate, and intra‑abdominal body
temperature were analyzed with repeated measures
analysis of variance (ANOVA). Repeated measures ANOVA
was applied to the measured data using a mixed model
including time, dose, and the interaction of time × dose as
fixed effects; baseline (pre‑dose) as a covariate; and animal
as a random effect to investigate chronological data. In cases
where the dose or interaction of time × dose was significant,
Student’s t‐test was conducted for each time point. A
probability of <0.05 was regarded as statistically significant.
SAS system for Windows, Release 9.3 (SAS Institute, Inc.,
Cary, NC, USA) was used for these statistical analyses.
Results
Thromboembolic stroke model and neurologic deficit score. At
1 h after embolization, all eight thromboembolic stroke
animals showed decreased consciousness level (score 8:
conscious but clouded and accepting; or score 10: drowsiness
but aroused with stimulation). In the sensory system, they
showed absent or decreased contralateral facial sensation,
pinna reflex, and pain response (score: 9 or 11). Motor
system impairment included paralysis of the contralateral
hand, leg, and upper limb (score 16). Additionally, skeletal
muscle coordination was affected, with animals unable to
walk (score 10: stand spontaneously but fall within a few
steps; or score 12: sit, just able to circle). At 6 h after
embolization, obvious changes in the neurologic deficit score
from those at 1 h after embolization were not observed in
any animal. In five thromboembolic stroke animals, the

experiment was terminated due to reaching a humane
endpoint for moribundity between 7 and 20 h after
embolization (7, 10, 12, 14, and 19 h after embolization) and
classified as moribund. In the other three animals treated as
non‑moribund animals, the neurologic deficit score at 24 h
after embolization was unchanged from the score at 1 h after
embolization (Table I).
Changes in blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and
body temperature of non‐moribund monkeys after
embolization. In normal animals, decreases in blood
pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature
were noted during the dark period (19:00 to 7:00, lights off
in the animal room) when compared with the pre‑time
point (9:00), and the circadian rhythm of the physiological

parameters during the light‑dark cycle was confirmed. In
non‑moribund thromboembolic stroke animals, blood
pressure (especially systolic) and heart rate increased from
1 h after embolization; these changes persisted until 24 h
after embolization. Respiratory rate increased significantly
between 3 and 10 h after embolization when compared
with the normal animals. Body temperature remained at
around 38˚C from 3 h after embolization, and statistically
significantly high values were noted between 7 and 20 h
after embolization (mainly the dark period) (Figure 1).
Changes in ECG waveforms and parameters of non‐
moribund monkeys after embolization. In the normal
animals, there were no changes in PR interval, QRS
duration, or QTc from the pre‑value. QT interval slightly
increased during the dark period, corresponding to
slightly decreased heart rate in this period. In the non‑
moribund thromboembolic stroke animals, there were no
differences in PR interval or QRS duration when compared
with the normal animals. Shortened QT interval and QTc
were noted after embolization, corresponding to a high
heart rate (Figure 2).
Differences in blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate,
body temperature, and ECG waveform changes after
thromboembolic stroke onset between non‐moribund and
moribund animals. In moribund thromboembolic stroke
animals, slightly higher values in blood pressure and heart
rate than in the non‑moribund thromboembolic stroke
animals were noted. Respiratory rate significantly
increased from 1 h after embolization; this change
persisted until 6 h after embolization. In body temperature,
there was no difference between the moribund animals
and non‑moribund animals at 3 h after embolization;
however, decreased body temperature was noted in
moribund animals from 4 h after embolization (Figure 3).

In the moribund thromboembolic stroke animals, no
abnormal rhythm or waveforms were observed until 6 h
after embolization. Before the animals became moribund,
premature ventricular contraction, sinus arrhythmia,
atrial fibrillation, and ST segment elevation were observed
(Figure 4).
Discussion
This study demonstrated that thromboembolic stroke in
cynomolgus monkeys led to increased blood pressure, heart
rate, and respiratory rate following embolization, with these
changes persisting for 24 h. Elevated respiratory rate and
body temperature at night, indicating possible circadian
rhythm disruption, were also observed. Several animals
exhibited moribundity 7 h after embolization or later;
compared to non‑moribund animals, higher blood pressure,
heart rate, and respiratory rate from 1 h after embolization
and lower body temperature from 3 h after embolization
were noted in these animals. In ECG, no changes in
waveforms or rhythms were observed in the animals after
embolization; however, premature ventricular contraction,
atrial fibrillation, and ST segment elevation were observed
in the thromboembolic stroke model before moribundity.
After stroke onset, human patients demonstrate
elevated systolic and diastolic blood pressures (15‑17),
both of which appear to rise acutely at the time of stroke
(18). Blood pressure then falls over the next 7‑10 days (16,
19), with most of this fall occurring within the first 1‑2
days (20). The changes are considered to be related to the
impairment of cerebral autoregulation (21), but the
mechanism is unclear. Elevated heart rate (22, 23) and

body temperature (24, 25) have also been reported in
stroke patients; the mechanism of these changes is
associated with autonomic nervous system dysfunction
(26) after ischemic stroke. In a middle cerebral artery
occlusion rat stroke model, cardiovascular disturbances
after ischemia were caused by autonomic changes
innervated by the insular cortex via the amygdala (27). In
our monkey stroke model, the infarct extended from the
basal ganglia to the lateral sulcus and insular cortex (10,
11, 14). This infarct was considered to have caused cardiac
function disturbance such as premature ventricular
contraction, atrial fibrillation, and ST segment elevation.
Most hemodynamic variables, including systolic blood
pressure, diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pulse
pressure, and heart rate, have been associated with
functional outcomes after acute ischemic stroke (28).
Elevated blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate
in acute ischemic stroke have been associated with more
severe strokes, worse functional outcomes, and early
death (28‑31). Patients who deteriorated had more severe

strokes, higher mortality, and significantly lower body
temperature on admission (32). The higher systolic and
diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate
and lower body temperature noted in the moribund
thromboembolic stroke model animals demonstrated that
our model reflects the symptoms of acute human stroke.
These physiological parameters can therefore be used to
predict clinical outcomes and as criteria for humane
endpoints in efficacy pharmacology studies evaluating

drugs using a thromboembolic monkey stroke model.
The most common changes in ECG reported in patients
with acute ischemic stroke include T wave inversion, QTc
prolongation, sinus bradycardia, and ST segment
depression (33). Changes in ECG can be considered as an
independent factor predicting 1‑year mortality of patients
with ischemic stroke (34‑36). In the present study, there
were no ECG abnormalities in rhythm or any parameter in
the thromboembolic monkey stroke model, except for
moribund animals, until 24 h after ischemia. In the clinic,

later (35), whereas in the present study, the evaluation
period was the ultra‑acute phase of 0 to 24 h after the onset
of cerebral ischemia, which may have been why ECG
changes were not observed in the thromboembolic stroke
model. In the moribund thromboembolic stroke model
animals, premature ventricular contraction (PVC), sinus
arrhythmia, atrial fibrillation, AV block, and ST segment

elevation were observed before moribundity; these changes
were conceivably due to 1) myocardial ischemia induced by
increased heart rate associate with autonomic nervous
system dysfunction and 2) electrolyte abnormalities
induced by worsening of general conditions.
In conclusion, we observed elevated blood pressure,
heart rate, and respiratory rate in a thromboembolic
monkey stroke model and demonstrated that these
changes may exacerbate stroke outcomes. They were
similar to post‑stroke cardiovascular complications in
humans known as SHS. Our model could be applied in the
development of therapies for managing post‑stroke
cardiovascular complications.
